en: Preface to the *Zongmen Baoji Lu*:
The presence of the ancient worthies (*gude*) within the Śākya tradition is like that of the former scholars (*xianru*) within our own school of learning.

Just as the former scholars used recorded sayings (*yulu*) to elucidate the lost scriptures of the Sages, the ancient worthies used recorded sayings to expound the profound meanings of the Tathāgata. In establishing their fundamental tenets...
Instruction proceeds from the source to the current and from the root to the branches; its Way is one and the same. To speak of the former Confucian scholars:

beyond the specialized schools of the Han dynasty masters such as Mao, Zheng, Jia, and Fu who lectured on the Classics, there were other works by scholars in the Confucian tradition that frequently corresponded with or diverged from the Six Classics.
Furthermore, following Zhou, Cheng, Zhang, and Zhu, there was, for instance, Tai...
Books such as the *Jitong*, *Zhengmeng*, the two inscriptions on the East and West walls, the *Quanshu*, and the *Yulei* are particularly numerous, beyond counting.
Yet, until now, one has never heard of anyone who took the discussions of the former scholars, categorized them by type, and appended them to the end of the sages’ scriptures.
It was not until the *Zhengyi* of the Tang dynasty and the *Daqian* of the Ming dynasty that these various works were finally compiled and assembled.

He compiled these works into a single collection and synthesized their essential points; yet even those with discernment still offered criticism, contending that with the rise of the *Zhengyi* (Correct Meaning), the learning of the Han scholars had begun to perish, and with the production of the *Daqian* (Great Compendium), the learning of the Song scholars was likewise lost. This was because his book excerpted and appropriated [passages] from various sources.

If one strives to harmonize everything according to the views of a single individual, then although the names of the various Confucian scholars of the Han and Song dynasties may remain, they will merely become "Han Confucians" as seen by Kong Yingda or "Song Confucians" as seen by Yang Rong;

this is certainly not as good as preserving each work individually. In the latter case, the person's character is complete and their spirit is fully revealed, enabling future generations [to understand them].
Reading it, it is as if one were receiving their very breath and hearing their instructions. Alas!
Even those with the learning and talent of Kong Yingda and Yang Rong could not avoid this defect; how much more so for those who fall far short of these two masters?
Therefore, I maintain that those who compile the recorded sayings of former scholars should merely eliminate redundancies, in order to...

To capture the true essence of a person and compile the recorded sayings of the ancient virtuous ones, one need only eliminate the redundant and the superfluous to preserve what is authentically theirs.

It is certainly not necessary to elevate them to the rank of the sages' scriptures or to affiliate them with the lineage of the Tathāgata before they can be considered the transmission of the Water of Si River or the orthodox pulse of Mount Ling. — Xi Shu Xiao Tang Xi He.
Shang was young when he studied the Confucian classics and grew up to master the Buddhist vehicle. He received the true transmission of Hongjue and succeeded to the Dharma seat of Tiantong.
Having once been summoned by imperial decree to preside over Long’an, he became a model for scholars from all quarters; yet he lived with but a single ladle and a single robe, drifting like clouds.
His gaze toward the heavens reveals a clarity no different from that of the ancient masters.

Were he to stand within the grove of the various Confucian scholars, the extent of his learning and insight would not merely allow him to follow in the footsteps of Zhongda (Wang Chong), but would surely place him in equal carriage with Yuan Ren.

Upon examining the *Zongmen Baoji Lu* (Record of the Jewel Accumulation of the School Gate) which he composed, one finds it concise, appropriate, precise, and exact—a work that has served as a standard for all [scholars] since the Song, Yuan, and Ming dynasties.

The voice, laughter, and countenance of the Elder appear as if one were seeing them in person; this is not like those who merely rely on the ancestral lamp to wield the brush and parade their extensive learning.

Therefore, I have specifically set forth his grand and upright intent, which may indeed serve as a model for writing within the Confucian tradition—how could it be of benefit to the ancient masters alone?
In the middle of the third month of the late spring of the Jiwu year of the Kangxi era,
[this was written by] the Imperially Presented Graduate and First-Rank Graduate,

Grand Master for the Second Class with Provisions, Lecturer at the Imperial Study, Recorder of Court Proceedings, Director of the Hanlin Academy, concurrently serving as Minister of the Ministry of Rites.
Written by Xu Yuanwen of Kunshan, promoted one rank, with humble prostrations.
Preface to the *Zongmen Baoji Lu*.
I have heard that the ancient Buddhas taught that in this Sahā world, the essence of the Dharma consists of pure sounds. Therefore, when [the teaching] first came from the West...

Although the intent of transmitting the mind sought to sweep away all phenomena and avoid falling into verbal explanations, the various masters—whose minds were sealed with one another—each possessed verses of realization.
Contemporaneous scholars transcribed these and treasured them as repositories;
furthermore, they carved them into various volumes to circulate them widely, and thus the *yulu* (recorded sayings) came into being. This was like relying on a boat when crossing a river.
Boats and oars are what those who seek fish and rabbits must necessarily rely upon as their traps and snares. Now, the fundamental substance of the mind is itself the nature (*prakṛti*).

Not a single dharma is established, yet the myriad functions are fully manifest; utterly detached from the sense bases and their objects, the true mechanism alone is revealed. Its subtlety and profundity are ultimate.
Nevertheless, sentient beings are entangled by emotional perceptions and rarely able to dwell securely in right concentration (*samyak-samādhi*); thus, [the Master]...

The masters of antiquity established points of doubt and employed the arts of concession, seizure, killing, and enlivening to strip away all attachments and enable their disciples to break through to liberation.
Reaching down to the present day, those capable of skillful reflection have realized its dynamic function within their own minds;
such is its wondrous nature. I pay reverent homage to this.
His Majesty Emperor Shizu (Chang Huangdi), riding upon the vow of merit from the celestial palace, held the Golden Wheel to govern all under heaven.
The profound benevolence and abundant grace he gradually spread were as vast and deep as the transformation of the Tathāgata’s Dharma;

furthermore, his wisdom of self-awakening through many lifetimes accorded perfectly with the wondrous mind of *nirvāṇa* of that very day. During a moment of leisure amidst the myriad affairs of state...

At that time, Master Youguan Huihai raised aloft and fully expressed the winds of our school’s fundamental doctrine. Celestial light descended from above, illuminating the sands of the Ganges everywhere.

Among all those who had their hearts perfumed and their ears attuned, there were none who did not receive his compassion and be moistened by his grace—no different from the spring thunder and timely rain that cause the buds and shoots of the myriad plants to open and flourish, leading them to full splendor. At that time, Chan Master Hongjue Minguo was just then, by [the decree of] Heaven...
The eldest legitimate son of a youth, he presides over the Dharma in the southeast.
Having come here by imperial decree, he has repeatedly received the Emperor’s inquiries;

not only does his wondrous realization accord perfectly with the sagely intent, but when confronting difficult challenges, his eloquence is as swift as a galloping wind, and in the intervals between his compositions, his literary brilliance is as radiant as the morning clouds.

Indeed, there remains the lingering fragrance of the Stone Gate and North Ravine [monasteries]. His foremost disciple who attained the Dharma, Upādhyāya Xiao Tang, possessed a realization so transcendent that he held the whisk in the Master’s stead and entered the inner chamber of the teaching hall;
this was much like Yuanwu’s delight in the presence of Dahui, where their insights met like the points of needles.
At that time, I attended his Dharma assembly and was fortunate enough to hear the true meaning, though I have not yet been able to manifest it before me.

I was awakened to this realization. Yet my heart remained filled with a sense of longing; recognizing the subtle point of return, I shut myself away in seclusion to contemplate its entry, only to find it even more inaccessible than before.

On occasion, I have perused the *Lamp Records* (*Denglu*), seeking to exhaustively investigate the functional mechanisms of the ancients, yet I could not help but lament that I had not seen the complete collection.
Now that the Master has long since entered into nirvana and I too am old, I have finally...

After Master Xiao returned from the south, he followed the late instructions of Meditation Master [Fengxue] to collect the recorded sayings (yulu) of ancient worthies from the Tang and Song dynasties, as well as those masters who appeared during the Yuan and Ming periods.
He compiled these into a single volume, gathering all that had not been previously published or was incomplete.
This work is titled *The Precious Accumulation Record of the Zen School*. Having been presented to me from a thousand miles away, he requested that I compose a preface for it.

As I reflect on the present while tracing back to the past, I savor the joy of Chan and my dharma-joy increases. Forgetting my own stubborn ignorance and meager learning, I am willing and eager to offer these words to assist in the cultivation of right faith;
yet, I feel ashamed that I have not been able to illuminate even a ten-thousandth part of the Dharma-gate of the Mind-Ground. Nevertheless, as for the *Ratnakūṭa*...
Does not the Sūtra say: "The eighty-four thousand vocal teachings expounded by the Tathāgata are all termed 'letters' (vyañjana).
To be free from all speech and written characters is termed 'meaning' (artha).

If a student records this and is able to contemplate it in such a way, then even in a place where there is no path of meaning, they will see their own essence directly. Thus, the jewel-robe lost over kalpas will be found without seeking.
Spontaneously, in the mere twinkling of an eye, all manner of household treasures flowed forth. How joyful this is!
Thus we know that Master Xiao’s diligent compilation was truly a worthy succession of his predecessors' aspirations, bringing forth the luster of the hidden virtues of the ancient masters.
His contribution to this Way is indeed no small matter.
Written on the mid-winter month of the year of Guihai in the Kangxi era, by Wang Xi of Wanping, who offers his prostrations with reverent bath.
The Reverend Xiao Tang of Tiantong has recently completed the compilation of his *Zongmen Baoji Lu* (Precious Accumulations of the Zen School).

He requested that I write a preface for it. I declined, saying: "This is the bloodline of the Chan school, recorded by those of its noble lineage; all its contents pertain to the primary truth (*paramārtha*).

As one who studies Confucianism, I have not been able to peer even into its fundamental tenets; how could I dare to compose a preface? Nevertheless, I have often examined the origins and development of the Śākya teachings."
The *Sūtra in Forty-two Sections* first began to be transmitted during the Eastern Han dynasty; by the time of the Two Jin dynasties, its followers had become increasingly numerous.

Among the renowned scholars of the Jiangzuo region at that time, even those who prided themselves solely on their literary elegance would, when it came to analyzing the source of principle, necessarily seek out such figures as Master So-and-so or Daoist So-and-so.
Whenever they set forth various doctrines, they would invariably produce several hundred words, or even up to several thousand characters. Like flowers...

It shines forth with brilliant clarity. It is a pity that he did not record these as a formal discourse (yulu). Nevertheless, in his discussions of principle, he esteemed the *Xiaojing* and the *Laozi* alongside the *Prajñāpāramitā-sūtra* and the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*;
he treated the *Great Changes* (*Yijing*) as equal to the "Free and Easy Wandering" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*. His writings were already exceedingly ornate and profuse;
yet the various members of the Buddhist community, with their profound and incisive diction, vied with these famous scholars for eccentricity and refinement without ceasing.

Consequently, they eventually reached a stalemate. Thereupon, Bodhidharma of Western India had no choice but to come across the reeds, pointing directly to the original nature as the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye (*Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-kośa*).
He completely swept away all words and language; the cataracts were rolled back and the gloom cleared, and the sun shone forth brilliantly.
From this point on, he caused the two schools of Confucianism and Buddhism to each return to their own respective studies, and thus their debates gradually ceased.

The same applies here; I have personally verified this myself. Generally, among all things that differ from one another, they invariably alternate in rising and falling, just as cold and heat, day and night, come and go, waxing and waning—a process clearly visible to the eye. Yet, this is not the case with the two traditions of Confucianism and Buddhism.
As the Tang man said: "The Way of the Sage rested during the Jin and Song dynasties and was revived in the Tang. Since the time of the former Master Meng (Han Yu)...

Master Sheng requested to be enrolled among the disciples of Confucius and praised the Way of Mencius to the utmost. When the lineage of the Six Classics had fallen into ruin, it was revived from its vast obscurity;

likewise, within the School of the Buddhas, from the First Patriarch through the sixth generation down to Caoxi, the "separate transmission outside the teachings" blossomed throughout the world—this is the first instance of their shared flourishing.
Furthermore, when the great Confucian scholars of the Song dynasty emerged, they secretly elucidated the Mind-essence and began to clarify it.
While this school flourished, the Chan (Zen) tradition also reached its great height.
As Zhang Wending remarked, masters such as Mazu, Fenyang, Xuefeng, and Yantou were all gathered under the Buddhist fold; this was another instance of their simultaneous prosperity.
After Zhu Xi and Lu Jiuyuan, their respective schools gradually diverged, leading in recent times to the learning of the Yangjiang school and the learning of the Jushan school.

Furthermore, the Holy Path flourished once more; the Chan school also saw its single lamp continue from the end of the Yuan dynasty until later, when the elders Boshan Liaoxian, Shengchen, Tiantong Juexin, Qingshan Xuyun, and Jingshan Xinxing emerged from Houdong, causing the world to tremble with spiritual resonance once again—this is the first instance of simultaneous flourishing.
From this, we know that the two gates of Confucianism and Buddhism are not distinct.
Waxing and waning. Truly, by each clarifying their own original mind, one attains the ultimate Way. To the people of the world, Tianliang is in the south and Tianshu is in the north;
their radiance illuminates one another. Mount Song and Mount Hua stand tall and majestic, both equally revered.
This is what is meant by "the Way proceeding side-by-side without contradiction. Master Xiaotang was the eldest grandson of National Teacher Wuzu and the elder master Shanweng.
The Great Disciple presided over the Heavenly Youth Hall. Zhenyin was the third-generation successor.

Initially, Master Xiao received the command of the Elder Shangu to compile the recorded sayings (*yulu*) of various Chan masters from the Song and Yuan dynasties onward; he edited out the redundancies, extracted the essentials, and compiled them into this Great Collection.
To supplement what was not fully prepared in the various writings of the venerable masters of the *Huìyuán*, this task is indeed no easy matter.
For the True Eye and the Wondrous Mind are transmitted through a smile; yet, if one wishes to transmit them to the world, they must ultimately be entrusted to written words.

This requires that later generations be able to directly extract the wondrous essence of their predecessors with the very eyes and mind of the Master, leaving no further place for hidden secrets. And...
Only later was this book finally able to be transmitted. This is not something that can be seen through ordinary metaphors or explanations.
It is like extracting fat from within jade; like extracting marrow from within stone; like straining out the four great precious jewels from the vast ocean;
like first drawing the *aṅga* juice when purifying water; like gathering the "night-light" and "cavity-piercing" fungi from among the myriad herbs; and like using a crystal cup alone...
It is like filling a vessel with lion’s milk; it is as if, having obtained the sword of Tai, one brandishes it once and the heads of Jin and Zheng are all turned white.
It is like entering Qin and taking nothing else, but exclusively collecting the historical records and maps. It is like galloping up Mount Chang and already having secured the precious tally.

It is further like a single dot on a dragon’s eye, leaping up as if about to dance. It is like looking at a painting of water on a wall, where the current seems about to surge forth. It is also like counting...
To recognize half the face of the fan’s door after ten years is like discerning Xia Fu from amidst smoke and charcoal;
this is solely due to the mental eye of our Master Xiao. Whatever he points to is a star, and whatever he unfolds is a treasure.

This is sufficient to cause the fundamental nature of all the great elders of the past to be revealed in its vastness, their true countenances ultimately manifest, as if they were standing face-to-face with one another from the very moment the scroll is opened.
This letter shall suffice to be transmitted for ten thousand generations. That the Elder Mount Man (Shanweng Lao-ren) has entrusted this matter solely to you is truly a mark of great gravity.

I have therefore traced and recounted the flourishing traditions of both the Confucian and Buddhist schools, and I sigh at how this letter of yours reveals a capacity that even those who have abandoned all hope (icchantikas) could not yet manifest.
To be able to so faithfully inherit the will of your predecessors is indeed a world-treasure for the groves of the Śākya. This serves as the preface.
Written with prostrations by Li Yèsì Gǎotáng, a scholar of the Yongshang region:
As for the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, from the time the World-Honored One entrusted it to Kāśyapa until Bodhidharma’s arrival in the East, it has been a direct pointing.
The human mind realizes Buddhahood through seeing its nature; this is called the "Special Transmission Outside the Teachings" (*kyōge betsuden*), which does not rely on written words.
Although it is said not to rely on written words, the Way of direct pointing cannot be manifested without speech.

Therefore, Great Master Sengcan’s *Xinxin Ming* (Inscription on Faith in Mind) and the Sixth Patriarch’s *Platform Sutra* eloquently expound the school of mind, their waves ever more expansive. Subsequently, as the five schools were established side by side, the spiritual mechanisms became increasingly profound and steep.
Yet their chanting grew ever more lofty; like shooting stars and rolling thunder, their words were like a sudden clap of lightning that awakens the deaf.

These were compiled into the *Lamp Records*, the *Essentials of the Assembly*, and various treatises on Venerable Patriarchs. Subsequent learners have relied upon them, and those who "lost the cloth bag" (attained enlightenment) are beyond counting.
Truly, these are excellent remedies for raising the dead back to life; how can they be regarded merely as mere texts? However, the Way and the fortunes of the times—*lóng*... [text truncated]

It cannot be replaced. The majestic ancestral lamp has nearly reached the point where nine tripods hang by a single thread; yet those of dull faculties and superficial understanding have no way to enter its gate.
They even mistake literal words for the ultimate meaning, clinging to medical prescriptions as if they were the wondrous elixir.

It is not only that there is no evidence of their saving people; it will soon be seen that the harm they bring is no small matter. Fortunately, the ancient "frozen pus" (a derogatory term for those who have long been stagnant) has recently risen to save the world.
Using wedge to extract wedge, and using words to shatter words, his remarks for compensating deficiencies and remedying abuses are more than sufficient.

Since the publication of the recorded sayings of the venerable masters from the *Huìyuán* era, however, those who have followed in compiling such works have not been able to exhaustively complete them.

In compiling this complete collection, it is found that for the majority—perhaps eight or nine out of ten—of those eminent elders who rose to prominence, only their names remain while their records have vanished.
This is the case for such venerable predecessors as Huanglong Huinan, Dinglin, Xinyuan, and Xiatang, all of whom were renowned for their brilliant reputations that shook the world of their time;
yet today, when one seeks their complete recorded sayings, none are to be found. It appears that those who compiled these works merely gathered and excerpted fragments from them.
The *Yinghua* (Essential Blossoms) and the individual volumes of the collected works were lost amidst the wild smoke and overgrown weeds, and thus fell into oblivion.

Furthermore, with the shifting of mountains and valleys and the succession of wars and conflagrations, some texts have been preserved while others have perished; one cannot even know how many times this has occurred.
Consequently, scholars are unable to see the complete works of the ancients, and failing to do so, they cannot fully grasp the ingenuity of the ancients.
It is for this purpose that our late master, the Venerable Hongjue, felt profound compassion for this matter.
He wished to collect the extant records from the Song dynasty down to the present day—spanning approximately four to five hundred years—and compile them into a single work.

Regarding the structure of this compilation, he followed the precedent of the *Records of Ancient Patriarchs* (*Guzunsu Lu*), gathering the ancients together in one hall so that students might take them as their teachers, as if they were hearing them in person.
Coughing and clearing their throats, they gaze upon the mallet and fly-whisk, read the words, and contemplate the pivot of the teaching;

thus they experience a triggering of realization and awakening, like Lingyun seeing the peach blossoms, Xiangyan striking the bamboo, Dayuan hearing the painted horn, and Foguo listening to the cock crow.
If this is true even for mere objects, how much more so for the ancients, whose tongues were like thunder and whose mechanisms were like the edge of a sword—all of which are preserved herein.
Would they not have ensured that no one would lose their "cloth bag"?

If you can thoroughly perceive the ancients' application of these teachings here, you may then race alongside them across a thousand years. Thus, this book ought to be completed with all haste. —Collected by [Author’s Name]
Before even half was finished, he responded to the summons of the celestial script. Having failed to complete his work, he took up the remaining fragments and transmitted them to Xi, saying:
"You shall complete this. Alas! Time has slipped away; now more than twenty years have passed. Morning and night, I remain filled with reverence and trepidation.
Fearing lest I should fail the mandate of my late master, I began to take up the brush in the spring of the Bingchen year.

Through three cycles of winter and summer, I searched and gathered [the materials], finally obtaining the writings of eighty-eight individuals and completing ninety-three fascicles, which I entitled the *Zongmen Baoji Lu* (Record of the Jewel Accumulation of the School Gate).
This was to fulfill my predecessor's will; it also serves to ensure that the blind donkeys of the future shall extinguish the True Dharma Eye.
Thus one knows its source.
Written on the first day of the New Year in the Jiwu year of the Kangxi era by the Bhikṣu Shanxiao Benxi of Zhili in Xichuan.
Regarding the compilation of the *Tiantong Dajian Tang Zongmen Baoji Lu* (The Tiantong Great Mirror Hall Record of the Precious Accumulation of the Chan School):
This work was edited by my late teacher Hongjue, who observed that the recorded sayings of the various patriarchs from the late Song through the Yuan and Ming dynasties were numerous.
These works were lost and no longer transmitted, causing the Dharma-gifts of the ancient masters not to shine forth to benefit the world;

this was held to be the fault of later students. Therefore, I commanded Xí to extensively seek them across various records and compile them into a single volume, titled *The Jewel Accumulation of the School Gate*.
May those who obtain this book regard it as having acquired a multitude of treasures; may they also know that the life of wisdom has its destination and that its profound source has its origin.
I only regret that my collection was not exhaustive and that many omissions remain. I can only hope that like-minded colleagues in the future will supplement and complete this great achievement.
The format for this collection follows entirely the precedents set by the records of the ancient patriarchs and masters.

It includes only such materials as formal sermons (*shàngtáng*), instructions to the assembly (*shìzhòng*), small-scale discourses (*xiǎocān*), recorded encounters (*jīyuán*), verses on cases (*niànsòng*), and dharma talks (*fǎyǔ*). As for other miscellaneous writings, they are so voluminous that it has not been possible to include them all in full.

Regarding the genealogical lineages of successive dynasties, the order of generations is not listed, nor are they divided into five branches. This is because all five schools originate from a single patriarch;

why then should they be partitioned into separate houses? Only beneath the titles of the volumes have I briefly appended the number of generations from Dajian (Huineng) for the sake of easy reference, so that readers may know their respective origins.
Generally, those already included in the records of the venerable patriarchs are not recorded again here.
However, Nan-yueh Hui-let and Ching-yüan Hsing-ssu are recorded once more to demonstrate that the continuous transmission under Ta-kuan did not extend beyond these two branches.

From Dajian (Huineng) down through the lineage from Nanyue to the twelfth generation, Yangqi Huai, as well as the fourteenth generation, Wuzu Yan, and other records are all fully contained within the *Zunsu Lu* (Records of Venerable Elders).

However, the records of the elders Xuefeng, Xuansha, Xiuyu, and Baiyun exist only as single-volume texts and have not yet been included [in the standard collections]. Therefore, this compilation begins from the lineages descending from Nanyue and Qingyuan.
The *Record of Chan Master Xuefeng Cun* is like the records of Yuanwu, Dahui, and Zhongfeng, which have long been included in the Tripitaka and widely distributed;

therefore, it is not included here. The records of Xuefeng, Xuansha, and the various patriarchs of the late Song dynasty have undergone repeated selection and editing and have circulated for a long time; therefore, [they are likewise not included].
I have removed only those miscellaneous writings; all else remains as it was.

As for the records of various Chan masters from the Yuan and Ming dynasties, as well as our own dynasty, they are so numerous that they would require oxen to carry them and fill entire buildings. Therefore, I have eliminated the redundant and selected the essential, compiling their general outlines.
I do not dare to exercise personal bias in my selection, nor to arbitrarily decide what to include or exclude.
This compilation was originally intended to gather the recorded sayings (yulu) of the various patriarchs;

it is not comparable to works such as the *Chuan deng lu* or *Xu deng lu*, which were compiled with the specific intent of investigating and verifying genealogical lineages and ancestral records. Therefore, those whose recorded sayings exist in the world have been included.
As for those who lack such records, I did not dare to include their names alone.
Among the various Chan masters mentioned in this book, there are those for whom stele inscriptions composed by eminent scholars or renowned elders have been appended;
their surnames and origins are not recorded again at the beginning of the volume, and their sermons and other discourses are recorded in full.
The various records of recent times conclude with the lineages descending from Yuan’an Yu, Juelang Sheng, and my late teacher Hongjue and his brothers.
Although these men were numerous and eminent, they have not yet been fully enumerated in this general history; I await future gentlemen to arise and compile them.
May those of lofty wisdom grant me their understanding and forgiveness.
The details of his dharma heirs are unknown. He once resided at Nanjian, where he compiled the *Xudeng cunmao* (Drafts for the Continuation of the Lamp), which has circulated in the world;
thus, they shall not be recounted here again. *General Principles of the Zongmen baoji lu* (Precious Accumulations of the Chan School Record).
